item.title: Peace Through Strength, Taiwan President Says on China Battle Anniversary
item.description: By Ben Blanchard and Yi-Chin Lee Peace can only be secured through strength and not even an inch of territory can be sacrificed, Taiwan President Lai Ching-te said on Sunday, visiting a sensitive frontline island to mark a key battle with Chinese forces almost seven …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Ben Blanchard and Yi-Chin Lee

Peace can only be secured through strength and not even an inch of territory can be sacrificed, Taiwan President Lai Ching-te said on Sunday, visiting a sensitive frontline island to mark a key battle with Chinese forces almost seven decades ago.

Taiwan has controlled the Kinmen and Matsu islands, which lie just off the Chinese coast, since the Republic of China government fled to Taipei in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists. No peace treaty or armistice has ever been signed.

In heavy rain, Lai laid a wreath and bowed at a memorial park for the 68th anniversary of the 1958 clash with Chinese forces, known as the start of the second Taiwan Strait crisis — the last time Taiwanese and Chinese forces battled on a large scale.

Addressing veterans later, Lai expressed gratitude to those who “stood united and fought a bloody battle to repel Communist totalitarian aggression”.

“Our resolve to unite in defending national sovereignty and safeguarding peace across the Taiwan Strait must never waver,” Lai said. “Peace has never simply fallen from the sky.”

The 1958 battle proves “that peace is secured through strength,” he said, adding it was necessary to maintain “the spirit of never yielding an inch” of Taiwan, Kinmen and another group of islands, while continuously boosting military spending.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Close to China

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly denounced Lai as a “separatist”. He rejects Beijing’s sovereignty, saying only Taiwan’s people can decide their future, but has also offered talks with China.

Kinmen at its closest is less than 2 km (1.2 miles) from Chinese-controlled territory. In the 1958 battle, Chinese forces began more than a month of bombardment of Kinmen, along with Matsu, including naval and air battles, seeking to force them into submission.

Taiwan fought back with support from the United States, though the crisis ended in a stalemate. Taiwan observes August 23 every year as the date it fended off the Chinese attack.

China’s coast guard has since early 2024 conducted regular “law enforcement” patrols around Kinmen in Taiwan-controlled waters, to Taipei’s anger.

Referring to those patrols and other Chinese tactics, Lai said that for 68 years China had not stopped its “ambitions for external expansion for even a single day”, bringing “unease” across the Indo-Pacific.

Taiwan’s planned defence spending next year will exceed T$1 trillion ($30 billion) for the first time, the government announced on Thursday, and Lai said he hoped for strong support for the budget.

($1 = 31.8250 Taiwan dollars)

(Reporting by Ben Blanchard and Yi-Chin Lee)

item.title: China’s July Coal Output Falls to Pandemic-Era Levels in Wake of Deadly Accident
item.description: By Colleen Howe China’s coal output in July fell back to pandemic-era levels, statistics bureau data showed on Monday, as stepped-up safety oversight after a deadly mining accident continued to weigh on mining operations. Coal output in China, the world’s largest producer, fell 10.1% to 343.21 …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Colleen Howe

China’s coal output in July fell back to pandemic-era levels, statistics bureau data showed on Monday, as stepped-up safety oversight after a deadly mining accident continued to weigh on mining operations.

Coal output in China, the world’s largest producer, fell 10.1% to 343.21 million metric tons in July from a year earlier, the National Bureau of Statistics said.

That was the lowest standalone monthly output figure reported since September 2021. That excludes output for the months of January and February, which are reported as a combined figure to smooth out the effects of the Lunar New Year holiday, which falls in either month and also affects production.

“This round of production declines was not caused by a weakening in demand, but rather stemmed from the continuous tightening of domestic coal mine safety regulations,” analysts at Galaxy Futures said in a note.

In May, 82 people were killed in a gas explosion at the Liushenyu mine in Shanxi province, the deadliest mining accident in 17 years, forcing many mines in the coal-rich province to close for inspections.

An initial probe into the incident found that the mine was using hidden tunnels and fake doors to shield some areas of the mine from regulatory oversight, state media reported.

“Many mines have voluntarily reduced their production loads after resuming operations, with significant reductions in Shanxi province in particular,” the Galaxy Futures analysts said.

The analysts forecast a 7%-9% year-on-year drop in August coal production and a 3%-5% decline for the full year, as tighter scrutiny forces mines to curb their previously undisclosed production.

Output for January-July reached 2.7 billion metric tons, down 2.9% compared with the same period last year, the statistics bureau data showed.

(Reporting by Colleen Howe; Editing by Sonali Paul and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

item.title: Philippine Defense Chief Rejects China Criticism, Calls Response a ‘Squid Tactic’
item.description: Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro rejected on Saturday China’s accusation that he has “consistently attacked and smeared” Beijing, branding the remarks as a “classic squid tactic” aimed at avoiding the issues at hand. Teodoro was responding to Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, who on Friday said Teodoro …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro rejected on Saturday China’s accusation that he has “consistently attacked and smeared” Beijing, branding the remarks as a “classic squid tactic” aimed at avoiding the issues at hand.

Teodoro was responding to Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, who on Friday said Teodoro had previously led efforts by Philippine authorities to apprehend Chinese citizens who, Beijing said, were legally working in the Philippines.

“This individual has consistently attacked and smeared China,” Guo told reporters, referring to Teodoro. “What he is damaging is not only China-Philippines bilateral relations, but also the interests of the Philippine state and its people.”

Teodoro, in a statement, defended the May law-enforcement operation at a steel facility in Misamis Oriental that resulted in the arrest of Chinese nationals, saying it was lawful and supported by evidence gathered through court-issued search warrants.

He cited what he said were violations involving the production of substandard, radioactively tainted steel, the dumping of polluted water, and the release of toxic emissions.

He also accused Chinese embassy officials of intervening in Philippine law-enforcement processes and threatening retaliation against Filipinos, saying a Senate hearing had revealed such actions.

“The latest Chinese Foreign Ministry statement against me is a classic squid tactic – disinformation through avoidance,” Teodoro said.

The dispute follows China’s confirmation on August 10 that its immigration authorities had taken action against more than 100 Philippine nationals for illegally working or living in China. Beijing said the operations were lawful and that immigration officials acted in a “standard and civil manner” while protecting the rights of those involved.

Teodoro, in an August 13 statement, condemned China’s action against the Filipino nationals, describing it as “plain and simple extortion and blackmail.”

The latest exchange continues a deterioration in ties between Teodoro and Beijing. China imposed  sanctions  on him in June after he described China as a “severe threat” to the Philippines territorially and politically, prompting Teodoro to respond by calling China “wicked.”
